narrative:
**HEADLINE**  
Macro risk remains High, with copper supply pressures easing but financial leverage and critical-input vulnerabilities dominating the landscape.

**CHANGES**  
• **Copper & the electrification deficit** moved to Moderate (from 5.0). Copper deficit timing swung to surplus, offsetting elevated mine disruptions and prices; reduces near-term supply-chain squeeze but mask longer-term electrification constraints.

**ELEVATED OR HIGHER RISKS**  
Three stories at High: Japan fiscal/JGB/carry trade (systemic unwinding risk), Private credit's opaque expansion (leverage opacity and contagion), Critical minerals as a weapon (geopolitical supply control), AI power & grid bottleneck (infrastructure capacity), Sea lanes & undersea cables (chokepoint resilience).  
Seven stories remain Elevated, spanning Treasury basis trades, developing-world debt, China deflation spillover, CRE maturity walls, and commodity/input fragility.

**WATCH**  
Private credit's opaque expansion (level 8, High)—largest absolute risk, least transparent exit paths.

stories.name: Treasury basis trade (hidden leverage)

indicators.label: SOFR minus EFFR (%)
MOVE index (Treasury volatility)
SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)

stories.summary: Hedge funds run a highly leveraged arbitrage between Treasury cash bonds and futures. It is a major source of liquidity, but a spike in funding costs or Treasury volatility can force rapid unwinds, as briefly happened in March 2020 and again in 2025.

stories.name: Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade

indicators.label: USD/JPY (yen strengthening = lower = risk)
30-year JGB yield (%)
Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)

stories.summary: Decades of near-zero rates made Japan the funding leg of a vast global carry trade. As the BoJ normalizes and JGB yields rise, fiscal financing gets harder and carry unwinds can transmit stress worldwide - the August 2024 mini-crash was a preview.

stories.name: Private credit's opaque expansion

indicators.label: US high-yield OAS (%, ≈310bps)
Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)

stories.summary: Lending has migrated from banks to lightly regulated private-credit funds, where assets are marked infrequently and leverage is opaque. Defaults are rising from a low base; the risk is that losses surface suddenly rather than being visible in real time.

stories.name: Developing-world debt crisis

indicators.label: Broad US dollar index (FRED DTWEXBGS)
US 10y real yield (TIPS, %)
New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A strong dollar, high real rates, and heavy foreign-currency debt loads leave many developing economies vulnerable to a sudden stop. A cluster of sovereign defaults or new IMF programs would signal the slow-burn crisis turning acute.

stories.name: China's price spillover (deflation or cost-push)

indicators.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
USD/CNY (yuan depreciation = higher = risk)
New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)

stories.summary: China's factory-gate prices spill into global goods markets in BOTH directions: years of PPI deflation exported disinflation and squeezed competitors, while a sharp 2026 reversal to positive PPI (energy/commodity cost-push) now exports input-cost pressure. Either large swing is destabilising; the indicator is scored on the size of the move, not its sign.

stories.name: Critical minerals as a weapon

indicators.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)

stories.summary: China dominates the mining and especially the processing of rare earths and critical minerals, and has shown willingness to use export licensing as leverage. Supply chains for magnets and defense inputs have little near-term substitute.

stories.name: Stablecoins & Treasury demand

indicators.label: Largest stablecoin max peg deviation (%)
Total USD stablecoin supply ($bn)
GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Dollar stablecoins have become sizeable holders of short-term Treasuries, linking crypto plumbing to the funding market. A large redemption wave could force rapid T-bill selling; the GENIUS Act's implementation is the key regulatory variable.

stories.name: AI build-out circular financing

indicators.label: US investment-grade OAS (%) - big-issuer proxy
AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)

stories.summary: AI infrastructure spending vastly exceeds current AI revenue, increasingly financed with debt and circular vendor arrangements. If monetization disappoints or GPU-backed financing strains, the capex cycle could reverse sharply.

stories.name: CRE maturity wall / regional banks

indicators.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A wall of commercial real-estate loans - especially office - matures into higher rates and lower valuations, concentrated at regional banks. Rising delinquencies and 'extend and pretend' practices defer, rather than resolve, the losses.

stories.name: France / eurozone fragility

indicators.label: OAT-Bund 10y spread (%)
Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)

stories.summary: France combines a wide deficit, a fragmented parliament, and recurring budget standoffs, widening its spread over Germany. Political instability or a rating downgrade would test eurozone cohesion at its second-largest economy.

stories.name: Hidden consumer debt

indicators.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
US unemployment rate (%)
BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)

stories.summary: Beneath headline figures, subprime auto and buy-now-pay-later delinquencies are climbing, and the labor market is the swing factor. A rise in unemployment would convert stretched-but-current borrowers into defaults quickly.

stories.name: Gold / de-dollarization

indicators.label: Gold price (USD/oz)
USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)

stories.summary: Central banks are accumulating gold and building non-dollar settlement arrangements at the margin. It is a slow erosion rather than a sudden shift, but reserve 'weaponization' events can accelerate diversification away from the dollar.

stories.name: Insurance retreat

indicators.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
US single-family mortgage delinquency (%, FRED DRSFRMACBS)
Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)

stories.summary: Insurers are retreating from climate-exposed markets through non-renewals and exits, shifting risk onto homeowners and state backstops. Severe catastrophe seasons strain the system and feed into housing and mortgage stress.

stories.name: Pensions / demographics

indicators.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
Large public-pension funded ratio (%)

stories.summary: Aging demographics and underfunded public pensions create slow fiscal pressure, while leveraged liability-driven strategies can blow up fast - as the UK gilt/LDI crisis showed in 2022. Benefit-reform fights are the political pressure valve.

stories.name: AI power & the grid bottleneck

indicators.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)

stories.summary: Data-center electricity demand is colliding with multi-year grid interconnection queues and slow capacity additions. Whether this is an acute shortfall or eases depends on the pace of AI build-out versus new supply - forecasts diverge widely.

stories.name: Copper & the electrification deficit

indicators.label: Copper price (USD/lb, COMEX HG=F)
Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)

stories.summary: Electrification and AI infrastructure point to structural copper deficits as demand outruns new mine supply, which takes a decade to build. Price is the live signal; mine disruptions and inventory draws would confirm tightening.

stories.name: Water - the underpriced input

indicators.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)

stories.summary: Water is systematically underpriced yet essential to chip fabrication, agriculture, and power. Droughts in key hubs (Taiwan's fabs, major farming regions) and transboundary disputes can disrupt supply chains in ways markets rarely price in advance.

stories.name: Food & fertilizer fragility

indicators.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)

stories.summary: Food security depends on concentrated fertilizer supply chains - potash, phosphate, and gas-derived nitrogen - exposed to export curbs and shipping chokepoints. Curbs or input shocks feed through to prices with a lag.

stories.name: The lithography (ASML) chokepoint

indicators.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

stories.summary: ASML is the sole maker of EUV lithography machines, with Zeiss the sole optics supplier - a single point of failure for advanced chips. Export controls, retaliation, or any disruption to this chain would ripple across the entire tech economy.

stories.name: Sea lanes & undersea cables

indicators.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
WTI crude oil (USD/bbl, CL=F)
Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)

stories.summary: A few maritime chokepoints and undersea cables carry most global trade and data. The 2026 Hormuz/Red Sea disruptions showed how quickly closures spike energy and shipping costs; cable cuts are a parallel, under-watched vulnerability.

stories.name: Clearinghouses (financial chokepoint)

indicators.label: Equity volatility (VIX)
Treasury volatility (MOVE)
Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Central counterparties now concentrate the system's risk by design, and Treasury central-clearing mandates will route more activity through them. In a volatility spike, procyclical margin calls can amplify stress - they are a systemic single point of failure.

items.label: Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
items.rationale: Fitch's inclusive TTM default rate (counting distressed exchanges and liability-management exercises) ticked up one notch from the April-May record of 6.0% to 6.1% in July 2026, confirming the rubric anchor at 6.0% has been surpassed; the rate has held at or above 6.0% every month since April 2026, with maturity extensions under stress comprising the plurality of default events, consistent with elevated funding stress in private-credit plumbing.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings July 2026 US Corporate Distressed and Default Monitor: 'private credit defaults hit a record 6.1%' for the trailing 12 months ending July 2026, up from 6.0% in April-May 2026, per cryptobriefing.com citing Fitch's July 2026 report (published ~mid-August 2026); corroborated by angelinvestorsnetwork.com ('Fitch's most recent monthly update pegged it at 6.1% for the period ending July 2026') and FinancialJuice/X ('Fitch Ratings US private credit default rate remains at record high in July 2026', ~Aug 10 2026). Fitch's measure includes distressed exchanges and stressed maturity extensions.

dissent.view: LinkedIn/Fitch post title fragment: 'U.S. Private Credit Default Rate drops to 5.2% in July' — likely a sub-segment or alternative metric, not the headline inclusive TTM rate
Proskauer Private Credit Default Index: 2.51% in Q2 2026 across 716 senior secured/unitranche loans ($195.6B) — count-based, excludes many distressed exchanges
Moody's 2025 headline private credit default rate: 1.6%-4.7% excluding distressed restructurings; including them ~65% of defaults were exchanges/maturity extensions

items.label: Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: At least 7 named funds — including the three largest non-traded BDCs in the US (BCRED, Apollo ADS, Ares SIF) — simultaneously hit their quarterly repurchase caps in Q2 2026, with combined gated AUM well above $100B; this satisfies the rubric threshold for WIDESPREAD (>=3 of the largest funds, or gated AUM >$100B) with high confidence.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings data (cited by multiple sources, as of Aug 17 2026): 10 of 16 tracked non-traded BDCs breached their 5% quarterly repurchase caps in Q2 2026. Named funds with active gates in Q2: Blackstone BCRED (~$79B, gated June 4 on ~10% requests), Apollo Debt Solutions BDC (~$26B, 16.8% requests honoured at 5%), Morgan Stanley North Haven Private Income Fund (~$7B, 11.6% requests at 5% cap), Ares Strategic Income Fund, Blue Owl OTIC, Oaktree Strategic Credit Fund, Cliffwater CCLFX (~$31B). Robert A. Stanger & Co. puts Q2 repurchase requests at 12.4% of NAV — the highest on record — with sponsors fulfilling only 38%, leaving ~$9.6B unfilled (tradingmarketsignals.com, Aug 17 2026; ecmsource.com, Jun 24 2026; angelinvestorsnetwork.com, ~Aug 2026).

dissent.view: Early Q3 2026 data (Golub GCRED cleared July 29 tender in full at 4.8% of shares; first three NAV BDCs show Q3 requests at 4.6% vs 7.9% in Q2 for same funds) suggests redemption pressure may be peaking/easing in Q3, which would not change the Q2 WIDESPREAD reading but could lower the score in the next quarter

items.label: Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)
items.rationale: Cash clearing shows strong infrastructure progress (most members ready, majority of volume already clearing), but TBAC explicitly cited a documentation/legal backlog and pending exemptive relief for inter-affiliate and extraterritorial scope, and repo readiness lags materially -- these directly map to the rubric's FRICTION criteria (documentation backlog, pending exemptive relief). No further deadline extension or major operational failure has been reported, precluding a score of 2. [vintage guard: new read is 2026-07-27 data but the prior applied value was 2026-08 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: DTCC/FICC member survey (July 27, 2026): >$1.2 trillion in UST cash activity already clearing at FICC, ~$300-400B remaining; 79% of GSD netting members have account setups in place for Dec 31 2026 cash deadline. TBAC (May 2026) flagged 'legal and documentation issues remain a challenge' and that inter-affiliate and extraterritorial exemptive relief are unresolved; fewer than 1-in-3 firms 'very familiar' with done-away repo clearing models (SIFMA/DTCC pulse survey, Nov 2025, 330 firms). Sources: finadium.com/ficc-survey (DTCC, Jul 2026); home.treasury.gov/system/files/221/TBACCharge1Q22026.pdf (TBAC, May 2026); s203.q4cdn.com SIFMA pulse survey (Nov 2025).

dissent.view: DTCC/FICC characterizes the industry as 'well positioned' for Dec 31 2026 cash deadline and FICC clears >$12 trillion in avg daily transactions -- suggesting SMOOTH for cash leg

SEC filings (WVB All Markets Fund, 2026) cite 'substantial regulatory and operational uncertainties associated with implementation' for repo clearing, implying friction closer to PROBLEMS for the repo leg

items.label: AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
items.rationale: Capex growth (77-100% YoY) materially exceeds AI-revenue growth (82% Cloud at Alphabet; 123% AI run-rate at Microsoft), but AI-attributable revenue is sharply accelerating QoQ, not decelerating -- ruling out Score 2. No hyperscaler cut its AI-revenue outlook while raising capex; the gap is wide but not widening in the score-2 sense.
items.fact: Alphabet Q2 2026 (July 22 2026 earnings release, s206.q4cdn.com/alphabet): Google Cloud revenue +82% YoY to $24.8B (accelerating from +63% in Q1 and +48% in Q4 2025); quarterly capex $44.9B, ~doubled YoY; full-year capex guidance raised to $195-205B. Microsoft Q3 FY2026 (CNBC, April 30 2026): capex $31.9B +49% YoY; AI annualized revenue run rate $37B +123% YoY. Combined 2026 hyperscaler capex ~$725B, up ~77% YoY (valueaddvc.com, Aug 2026).

dissent.view: Alphabet Q2 FCF turned negative (-$5.9B first time in company history) and stock fell 7% on capex hike, suggesting market views gap as systemic and potentially score-2 severity
Moody's May 2026 flagged credit risk if 'strong profit growth from AI investments fails to materialise', implying widening concern beyond score-1

items.label: BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: Affirm 30+ DPD ran slightly above FY2025 levels for most of FY2026 (2.7%-2.8% range) before easing to 2.5% in Q4, indicating a mild YoY rise in delinquency; however, sector-wide charge-offs (~1.83%-2.0%) remain well below the 3% contained threshold and far below the 5% spiking threshold, placing this squarely in rubric level 1.
items.fact: Affirm Q4 FY2026 (fiscal year ended June 30, 2026): 30+ DPD on monthly installment loans (excl. Pay in X) = 2.5%, down from 2.7%-2.8% in prior three quarters but the FY2026 delinquency curve tracked slightly above FY2025 overall; BNPL sector charge-off rate ~1.83%-2.0% per Richmond Fed (Feb 2026) and CFPB data, well below 5%. Source: Affirm Q4 FY2026 earnings (Yahoo Finance/Investing.com, Aug 27 2026) and Richmond Fed Economic Brief EB-26-05 (Feb 2026).

dissent.view: BTIG Research (Aug 2026) flags Affirm ABS 2025-X2 vintage 30-59 DPD at all-time highs for newest vintages at 9 months of age, suggesting underlying credit deterioration beyond headline rates
Klarna global BNPL delinquency fell to 0.88% in Q2 2025 (down 15 bps YoY), and Klarna fixed-term delinquency also fell YoY, suggesting stable/improving trend for the sector's second-largest player

items.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
items.rationale: The most recent hard office-specific delinquency figure from an authoritative source is KBRA's 12.8% for February 2026; Trepp's own office sub-rate last recorded at an all-time high of 11.76% in October 2025, with July 2026 data indicating further deterioration from large office loan defaults. The rubric calls for the latest percent figure: 12.8 (KBRA Feb-2026) is used as the load-bearing fact, with the Trepp Oct-2025 figure of 11.76 as a floor-side dissent. [vintage guard: new read is 2026-02 data but the prior applied value was 2026-03 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: KBRA CMBS Loan Performance Trends: February 2026 (BusinessWire, 2026-02-27): 'The office delinquency rate decreased 110 basis points (bps) this month to 12.8%' among KBRA-rated U.S. private-label CMBS. Trepp-universe office rate hit a then-record 11.76% in October 2025 (CommercialSearch/Trepp); July 2026 Trepp report (MBA Newslink, 2026-08-11) shows overall CMBS DQ rose 51 bps to 7.86% with Chicago office tower and Seattle office portfolio among the largest newly delinquent loans, implying continued upward office pressure.

items.label: Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)
items.rationale: H1 YTD insured losses of ~$42-47bn are below (not above) the 10-year average of ~$66bn for H1, placing them far below the 150% threshold; the largest single event (~$5bn) is well below the $10bn trigger for ELEVATED. Rubric maps directly to 0=NORMAL.
items.fact: Swiss Re Institute (swissre.com, ~Aug 2026) estimates global insured nat-cat losses at USD 42bn in H1 2026, 16% below the USD 66bn long-term trend; Aon puts H1 at >=USD 47bn and Gallagher Re at >=USD 46bn, all below the 10-yr average. Largest single event was the April US SCS outbreak at ~USD 5bn insured (Aon). El Nino is suppressing the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season; no major US hurricane landfall recorded through late August 2026.

dissent.view: riskcoveragehub.com projects full-year 2026 losses tracking $115-135bn (above the $100bn annual threshold), implying H2 could be materially worse if a late-season hurricane or wildfire event materializes

items.label: GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)
items.rationale: The $4.2B refinancing wall, widening CDS spreads implying 50% five-year default probability, depreciated GPU collateral, and SOFR+550bps pricing on speculative-grade paper are clear 'SIGNS' of stress per the rubric (Level 1). However, CoreWeave successfully accessed markets (oversubscribed DDTL 5.5), and no confirmed default, distressed exchange, or failed refinancing has occurred, precluding Level 2.
items.fact: CoreWeave CDS markets priced a 50% five-year default probability as of July 29, 2026 (TechTimes/credit market reporting), against a $4.2 billion refinancing wall on pre-IPO GPU-backed debt due in 2026 (Dave Friedman Substack, April 2026) sitting against substantially depreciated GPU collateral. CoreWeave subsequently closed a $2.6B DDTL 5.5 at SOFR+550bps (Ba2/BB+ rated) in August 2026, but total debt reached $35bn as of June 30 2026 with net interest expense of $640M in Q2 alone (Capacity Global, August 2026). No confirmed default or failed refinancing has been reported.

dissent.view: JPMorgan and Global Data Center Hub characterize Q2 2026 AI infrastructure debt markets as healthy, with rating agencies granting investment-grade status to GPU-backed assets for the first time and deals pricing at record-tight spreads (e.g. Hut 8 Beacon Point at T+165)
SemiAnalysis (July 2026) frames Nvidia's GPU backstop program as a market-functioning liquidity mechanism, not a sign of acute distress, suggesting the neocloud financing ecosystem remains operative

items.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
items.rationale: Non-renewal waves are documented across all four US geographic regions encompassing well more than 15 states, satisfying the ACCELERATING threshold on headcount alone; however, NAIC simultaneously characterizes the market as 'operationally strong overall with improved underwriting results in 2024' and no top-10 insurer full-exit from a major state is confirmed in the primary source, so the most defensible single reading is RISING (5-15+ states, some markets stabilizing) rather than ACCELERATING.
items.fact: NAIC Aug 5 2026 report 'Examining Homeowner Property Insurance Market Dynamics: An Assessment of Countrywide State-Level Data From 2018 to 2024' (MCAS data, all four US regions) finds company-initiated non-renewal rates surged 96%-216% across ALL four geographic regions from 2018-2024; non-renewals per 1,000 in-force policies in the West tripled; Florida 2024 non-renewal rate 3.35% (highest nationally), California 3.18% (3.9x its 2018 rate); 715 companies active but more than half in each zone reduced policy counts. Insurer exits/pullbacks documented across Southeast, West (CA, FL, TX highlighted), Northeast, and Midwest - well above 5 states but NAIC characterizes overall market as 'operationally strong' with improved underwriting in 2024. No single top-10 insurer confirmed as fully exiting a major state as of report date. Source: NAIC MCAS Homeowners Insurance Report, Aug 5 2026 (content.naic.org).

dissent.view: climatecosmos.com (Jun 2026) lists 13 specific states with active non-renewal waves including CA, FL, TX, GA, OK and others, which on headcount alone could map to ACCELERATING (>15 states) if all counted; but this is a secondary, non-DOI source without hard insurer-exit confirmation.

NAIC MCAS report (Aug 5 2026) itself notes market 'remains operationally strong' with 715 carriers active and underwriting profit improved in every zone in 2024, supporting a STABLE or low-RISING read on systemic severity despite elevated non-renewal counts.

items.label: Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: At least 1-2 failures <$10bn in the trailing 6 months with at least one preceded by an FDIC enforcement action, and CRE is a credibly reported contributing factor for the January failure; this satisfies the ISOLATED threshold (>=1 enforcement action citing CRE, 1-2 small failures) without meeting CLUSTER criteria (no >=3 CRE-documented failures, no >$10bn failure, no coordinated interagency CRE action). [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]
items.fact: Five US bank failures recorded YTD 2026 per Forbes/FDIC data (as of ~Aug 24 2026). In the trailing 6 months (Mar-Aug 2026): Community Bank and Trust - West Georgia failed May 1 following an FDIC enforcement action in April 2026; Kentland Federal Savings and Loan failed Jul 10 as 'critically undercapitalized'; plus up to two additional unnamed failures. Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust (Jan 30, $261M assets) carried media-reported CRE ties but FDIC released no official causal statement (Bisnow, Feb 2 2026). No single failure exceeded $10bn assets; no coordinated interagency emergency action targeting regional-bank CRE stress was identified. FDIC 2026 Risk Review references CRE broadly. Source: Forbes Advisor (updated ~Aug 24 2026); Bisnow Feb 2 2026; FDIC failed-bank list.

dissent.view: Bisnow (Feb 2 2026) notes 'Regulators haven't publicly identified a direct cause' of Metropolitan Capital's failure, making any CRE attribution for that institution unofficial and media-inferred rather than confirmed by FDIC/Fed/OCC materials.

items.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
items.rationale: The Fitch ABS index is the authoritative primary source for securitized subprime auto 60+ DPD; the June 2026 reading of 5.67% is the most recent monthly figure available as of the report date, mapping directly to the rubric's requested percent. The rate peaked at a 32-year record of 6.90% in January 2026 and has since trended seasonally lower, now running below prior-year levels.
items.fact: The subprime 60+ day delinquency rate in June 2026 was 5.67%, down 64 basis points year-over-year, per Fitch Ratings subprime auto ABS index, as reported by Wolf Street on August 13, 2026.

dissent.view: Motley Fool/Globe & Mail (July 2026) characterizes the rate as 'around 6.8%' — this reflects the start-of-2026 (January-February) peak reading, not the more recent June figure.
Symend (June 2026 update citing Fitch) pinned the January 2026 rate at 6.9% as the reference figure; no more recent month cited.

items.label: Large public-pension funded ratio (%)
items.rationale: The Milliman 100 PPFI directly measures the 100 largest U.S. public defined-benefit plans on a monthly basis; 88.2% as of July 31, 2026 is the most recent, authoritative, directly measured figure and maps mechanically to the rubric's request for a representative large-plan funded ratio. Equable Institute's broader 253-plan universe shows 85.0% projected for FY2026, confirming the same order of magnitude but covering a wider, less concentrated set of plans.
items.fact: Milliman 100 Public Pension Funding Index (PPFI): funded ratio of the 100 largest U.S. public pension plans slipped from 88.7% as of June 30 to 88.2% as of July 31, 2026; total pension liability $6.911 trillion vs. plan assets ~$6.095 trillion. Source: Milliman PPFI, published August 27, 2026 (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260827829119/en/).

dissent.view: Equable Institute 'State of Pensions 2026' projects a national average funded ratio of 85.0% for FY2026 (as of June 30, 2026) across 253 statewide and municipal systems — broader universe and FY-end projection vs. Milliman's monthly mark-to-market of the top 100.

items.label: New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Bolivia and Guinea each represent genuinely new IMF program arrangements approved within the March–August 2026 window, satisfying the >=3 threshold when Ghana's new PCI is included; even on a conservative count of 2 financing programs, the rubric minimum for CLUSTER is met if Ghana is counted, pushing the score to 2. No new missed coupons or defaults were found, so distress is IMF-program-driven rather than payment-failure-driven.
items.fact: In the trailing 6 months, at least 2 new IMF financing arrangements were agreed: (1) Bolivia — new 36-month EFF (~$1.9bn), staff-level agreement July 29, 2026 (imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/07/29/pr26268-bolivia); (2) Guinea — new 41-month ECF, staff-level agreement Aug 11, 2026 (imf.org/en/news). Ghana additionally reached a new 36-month Policy Coordination Instrument (non-financing) in May 2026. No new sovereign missed coupons or defaults identified in the window.

dissent.view: Conservative reading excludes Ghana PCI (non-financing instrument) and counts only Bolivia + Guinea as 'new programs', yielding a count of 2 which maps to RISING (value=1) under a strict financing-only interpretation.

items.label: Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
items.rationale: All primary sources (ESMA June 2026, TPR March 2025) characterise LDI buffers as adequate and improved; no regulator has flagged a live liquidity crisis and no forced selling or central-bank intervention has occurred in 2026, placing this squarely in band 0 (NONE). The one residual ESMA caveat—that 'a subset of funds might still face challenges'—is a supervisory watch-item, not a formal stress flag meeting the band-1 threshold.
items.fact: ESMA TRV Risk Analysis dated 23 June 2026 found that 'the ability of funds to meet liquidity demands has improved compared to September 2022 after leverage-related measures under Article 25 of AIFMD were implemented,' driven by reduced leveraged exposures and a fall in LDI NAV to EUR 113bn end-2024 vs EUR 130bn at crisis. TPR's own market-oversight report (data to 31 March 2025) confirms LDI managers raised rate buffers to ~300 bps (from ~150 bps pre-2022), market size halved to ~£0.7tn, and no margin-call episode or forced selling has been reported in 2026. The most recent stress episode on record was the January 2025 gilt sell-off, which triggered cash calls described by eight industry advisers and BlackRock as 'orderly' with no forced gilt sales.

dissent.view: ESMA (June 2026) notes a subset of LDI funds may still face liquidity challenges under stress scenarios, suggesting residual tail risk not fully resolved

items.label: Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)
items.rationale: Active official rhetoric and a pre-summit pilot targeting for BRICS Pay and the gold-backed 'Unit' token qualify as Band 1 (TALK/new non-dollar settlement launches/rhetoric). No new sovereign reserve freeze or seizure in 2026, and no major economy has operationally moved reserve settlement off USD in an executed sense, so Band 2 is not triggered.
items.fact: As of 2026-08-31, BRICS Pay is targeted for a pilot launch at the 18th BRICS Summit (New Delhi, Sep 12-13, 2026), not yet held; BRICS finance ministers met in Jaipur on Aug 12-13 to prepare payment-system options (shabariseva.com, ~Aug 28 2026). No new sovereign reserve has been seized or frozen in 2026; the ~EUR 210-260bn Russian asset freeze is a 2022-era continuing rollover, not a new action. Russia's Deputy FM Ryabkov places BRICS Pay full operationality at 2030 (bricspayment.ru).

dissent.view: Some non-authoritative outlets (informedclearly.com, watcher.guru) characterize BRICS Pay as already 'operationally launched' in 2026 with 60-67% of intra-bloc trade in local currencies, which would suggest Band 2 proximity; however, these claims lack primary-source verification and contradict official BRICS Pay timelines and India's own public posture.

items.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
items.rationale: The trustees report materially worsened the OASI depletion date and the long-run deficit, and reform is actively debated with multiple bills introduced -- squarely DEBATE (1). No cut has been legislated or automatically triggered, so level 2 is not warranted.
items.fact: The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (released June 9, 2026, SSA.gov/OACT/TR/2026/) projects the OASI trust fund will be depleted in Q4 2032 -- one quarter earlier than last year -- with the 75-year actuarial deficit worsening from 3.82% to 4.42% of taxable payroll. Multiple bipartisan reform bills have been introduced (H.R. 9187 Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act; S. 4979 PROMISE Act) but none has been enacted; no automatic benefit reduction has been triggered.

dissent.view: CBO (Feb 2026) estimates a steeper 28% automatic cut at depletion vs. SSA trustees' 22%, reflecting differing economic assumptions -- same depletion date but larger implied cut

items.label: Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)
items.rationale: Anchoring on the corroborated Argus/Reuters x4–x5 range for dysprosium oxide (the primary HREE benchmark) and the mid-point of REEx-tracked bilateral transactions yields a central estimate of ~4.5× China domestic price; the Serra Verde $575/kg government-contract floor (~2.8×) is a hard lower bound, while $2,500+/kg extreme bilateral quotes (~12×) reflect opaque scarcity events rather than a liquid market clearing price.
items.fact: Dysprosium oxide trades at $204–210/kg inside China (ACREI index 259.1, Aug 18 2026) vs $575–$2,500+/kg in ex-China transactions per Rare Earth Exchanges; Argus data cited by Reuters (June 2026) puts dysprosium and terbium ex-China at x4–x5 domestic prices; Serra Verde DOD floor of $575/kg dysprosium implies ~2.8x floor multiple. Source: rareearthexchanges.com (Aug 18 2026); theoregongroup.com citing Argus/Reuters (Jun 10 2026).

dissent.view: Benchmark Minerals (Mar 24 2026) pegs the 2025 full-year average at 4.4× for dysprosium CIF North America, below current spot indications, suggesting the multiple has risen further in mid-2026
REEx (Aug 12 2026) documents ex-China dysprosium up to $2,500+/kg implying a ~12× premium at the extreme tail of bilateral transactions
Ucore (Feb 23 2026) cited ex-China dysprosium at ~$1,000/kg vs ~$200/kg China = ~5× multiple

items.label: Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
items.rationale: The rubric's Level 2 (RETALIATION) requires the target country to enact countermeasures; China's April 2026 State Council Order No. 834 and its Extraterritorial Jurisdiction Counter-Regulations are formal enacted legal instruments that directly counter the US/allied export-control push, satisfying that threshold alongside the US-side MATCH Act tightening measure.
items.fact: US lawmakers introduced the MATCH Act (April 2026) to ban DUV lithography exports to China and pressure allies including ASML's Netherlands; China responded with State Council Order No. 834 (April 2026) — a supply-chain security regulation authorizing legal action against companies harming Chinese supply chains — and separately promulgated 'Regulations on Countering Improper Extraterritorial Jurisdiction' enabling Beijing to deem FDP Rule compliance illegal. Sources: CSIS (https://www.csis.org/analysis/new-momentum-old-problems-transatlantic-export-control-considerations, June 2026); thenextweb.com (May 13 2026); JustSecurity (July 9 2026); Senate Foreign Relations Committee press release (April 8 2026).

dissent.view: The MATCH Act has not been enacted into law as of late August 2026 and remains in congressional committee; some analysts (East Asia Forum, March 2026) note the Trump White House is actually recalibrating toward softer chip controls to facilitate trade talks, suggesting the executive branch is partially offsetting legislative escalation — potentially capping this at Level 1.

China's Order No. 834 and counter-jurisdiction regulations are framework laws not yet actively enforced against specific companies like ASML, and the Dutch government has opposed the MATCH Act rather than implemented it — meaning neither side's measures are fully operational, which could support a Level 1 reading.

items.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
items.rationale: Transit volumes are severely reduced (~3-23% of normal depending on metric) and the strait is operationally contested with mines, naval stand-offs, and IRGC interdictions — but an active Iran-Oman de-escalation framework signed Aug 28 and some vessel transits still occurring cap the rating at 1 per the rubric. Brent at ~$88 is elevated (consistent with severe disruption) but not at the extreme closure-signal level seen at July peak ($105), and the rubric bars a '2' when any functioning convoy workaround or signed framework exists.
items.fact: EIA (Aug 11 2026 STEO) reports Hormuz oil throughput averaged 4.9 mb/d in Q2 2026 vs 21.6 mb/d pre-conflict (~23% of normal); ship-tracking data shows 3-15 vessel transits/day vs ~85-138 baseline; on Aug 28 Iran and Oman unveiled a Hormuz management framework (temporary corridor + joint mine-clearing); Brent crude ~$88/bbl as of Aug 30 — elevated but well below July peak of $105. Sources: EIA STEO Aug 11 2026 (eia.gov); straits.live Aug 30 2026; mightyshipping.com Aug 28 2026 update.

dissent.view: straits.live (Aug 30) and carraglobe.com label the strait 'effectively closed' citing only 3 transits on Aug 23 vs ~85/day normal, arguing volumes are well under 25% threshold for closure

Goldman Sachs (cited by global-energy-flow.com) estimates Gulf crude exports have recovered to ~two-thirds of pre-war levels via dark-shuttle trade, implying less severe effective closure than vessel-count data suggests
Trump administration claims mines are cleared and strait is open; denied by IMO and contradicted by ongoing tanker incidents per CNBC Aug 11 2026

items.label: New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)
items.rationale: Five or more confirmed distinct new major-economy trade measures (tariffs, anti-dumping orders, export controls) fall within the trailing 3-month window, satisfying the rubric threshold of >=4 measures for ESCALATING (2). Despite a nominal US-China truce framing, both sides have enacted concrete new unilateral measures in the period.
items.fact: At least 5 new major-economy trade measures against Chinese trade were enacted or formally announced in the June-August 2026 window: (1) USTR new 12.5% Section 301 forced-labor tariff on China, effective 24 Jul 2026 (China-Briefing, 23 Jul 2026; tariffstool.com); (2) EU definitive anti-dumping duty on Chinese polyamide yarns under Regulation EU 2026/1823, in force 27 Jul 2026 (cambioslegales.es, 28 Jul 2026); (3) China MOFCOM provisional anti-dumping measures of up to 54.3% on US/Mexican pecans, effective 11 Aug 2026 (Global Times / MOFCOM, 11 Aug 2026); (4) China MOFCOM Announcement No. 34 of 2026 tightening export controls on drones and components to the US, effective 5 Aug 2026 (Trivium China / fredgao.com, 6 Aug 2026); (5) China MOFCOM national-security investigation into foreign-software printers/copiers, launched 5 Aug 2026 (Trivium China, 6 Aug 2026). A further US 7.5% overcapacity tariff on China was signalled on 24 Aug 2026 (Bloomberg).

dissent.view: Some sources (cgoutdoor.com, Aug 2026) characterise the period as consolidation rather than fresh escalation, noting no new blanket tariff increase on all Chinese imports and framing activity as enforcement and review of existing measures; this would suggest RISING (1) rather than ESCALATING (2).

items.label: Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
items.rationale: Two rubric triggers for score 1 are both active simultaneously: (a) the truce expires Nov 10 2026, now <90 days away with no renewal signal, and (b) a partial breach occurred via entity-specific export control additions on Jun 22 2026, consistent with fraying rather than full collapse. Score 2 is not warranted because the blanket suspension remains formally in force and price signals do not corroborate a systemic reimposition of controls.
items.fact: China suspended its Oct-2025 rare earth export controls until Nov 10, 2026 (MOFCOM, Nov 7 2025; White House fact sheet Nov 1 2025). As of Aug 31 2026, that suspension is nominally in force but expires in <90 days with no announced renewal. Additionally, on Jun 22 2026 China added 10 US entities - including rare earth producers MP Materials and USA Rare Earth - to its export control list, barring dual-use exports to those firms (MOFCOM Announcement, June 22 2026; Reuters/Benchmark Minerals). Market reaction to the entity listings was muted (MP Materials roughly flat, USA Rare Earth modestly higher on announcement day), capping the read at partial breach rather than full lapse.

dissent.view: Some analysts (Benchmark Minerals, Al Jazeera, Bloomberg) characterise the Jun 22 entity listings as largely symbolic because targeted firms have minimal commercial exposure to Chinese inputs, which could support a score-0 (holding) read on the core truce.
Modern Diplomacy (Aug 21 2026) argues Beijing is 'preparing to let the truce expire' and frames the situation as closer to imminent lapse, which could support score 2.

items.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
items.rationale: The regime is squarely rubric-1: licensing is case-by-case or whitelist (general licences restricted to three named producers, not broad coverage), typical processing far exceeds 30 days (60-120+ days in practice), and new catalogue categories (samarium, gadolinium, lutetium compounds) were added in the 2026 licensing catalogue update within the trailing 3 months — all three rubric-1 triggers are present with no rubric-2 categorical denial or announced suspension of the core magnet licensing regime. [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]
items.fact: As of mid-2026, China's April 2025 MOFCOM controls requiring case-by-case export licences for seven heavy rare earth elements and derived magnets (SmCo, Dy/Tb-containing NdFeB) remain fully in force and were never suspended. General licences were issued in December 2025 to only three named Chinese magnet makers (JL MAG, San Huan, Yunsheng) and are 'not broadly available'; case-by-case applicants face 60-120+ day processing times far exceeding the 45-working-day statutory target. CSIS (May 5 2026) documents that U.S. imports of controlled elements such as yttrium fell from 333 tons to 17 tons over eight months and 'have never recovered to pre-restriction levels.' Sources: CSIS https://www.csis.org/analysis/rare-earth-export-restrictions-one-year-later (May 2026); blog.gettransport.com logistics guide (July 7 2026); Arnold Magnetics (Feb 2026); carraglobe.com (May 2026).

dissent.view: Multi-institutional analysis cited by Rare Earth Exchanges reports licensing approval rates below 25% for European firms and sixfold price spikes, implying near-frozen conditions closer to rubric-2; however this is a secondary aggregate estimate without a MOFCOM primary source and is not corroborated by a complete halt or announced categorical denial.

items.label: Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)
items.rationale: The rubric's Level 2 threshold requires <10% outside Taiwan AND no operational overseas leading-edge fab; both conditions are met with 0% operational <=3nm capacity outside Taiwan as of August 2026, all overseas <=3nm fabs still in construction or equipment-installation phase. Diversification is structurally underway but yields no current operational capacity relief.
items.fact: As of August 2026, TSMC has zero operational <=3nm capacity outside Taiwan. Arizona Fab 21 Phase 1 produces 4nm; Phase 2 (3nm) completed construction in April 2026 and began equipment installation Q3 2026 with volume production targeted 2H 2027 (TrendForce, March 2026; BlackRidge Research, 2026). Japan Kumamoto Fab 1 produces 22/28nm and 12/16nm; Fab 2 is under construction targeting 3nm with mass production expected 2028 (TSMC 2025 Annual Report; TrendForce April 2026). Taiwan holds ~150,000-180,000 wafers/month of 3nm capacity across Fab 18B phases, plus 90,000-100,000 WPM of 2nm ramping in Hsinchu/Kaohsiung (TrendForce April 2026; Global Semi Research Jan 2026). Outside-Taiwan share of <=3nm operational capacity: ~0%.

dissent.view: Some industry projections (Quantumrun, June 2026) forecast sub-2nm capacity splitting 70% Taiwan / 30% US by 2030, implying a near-term trajectory toward Level 1 by late 2020s, but this is a forward projection, not a current operational figure.

items.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
items.rationale: Episodic nearshore live-fire drills, coast guard jurisdictional probing, and assertive patrols match Rubric 1 (ELEVATED). No evidence of blockade, kinetic clash, or full mobilization rules out Rubric 2; activity clearly exceeds routine (Rubric 0) given live-fire and MSA jurisdictional moves.
items.fact: AEI China & Taiwan Update (Aug 14, 2026): PRC Guangdong MSA announced new maritime traffic control measures in the Taiwan Strait citing typhoon; PRC-Indonesia naval exercise east of Taiwan framed by state media as asserting PRC jurisdiction over Taiwan's eastern EEZ. Earlier (July 23-24, SCMP), PLA conducted a two-day live-fire drill in the Taiwan Strait, all zones within 12km of mainland coast, triggered by Lai Ching-te's 'not subordinate' remarks. The Diplomat (July 2026) reported no major PLA escalation in H1 2026 vs. late-2025, with H1 daily sortie average of 7.5 aircraft. No kinetic clash, blockade, or named large-scale encirclement exercise reported.

dissent.view: The Diplomat characterizes H1 2026 PLA pressure as 'generally stable' and tensions lower than end-2025, which could support a Rubric 0 (CALM) read for the broader trend even if specific episodes are elevated.

items.label: Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)
items.rationale: A named major cable (PEACE) is confirmed severed in the Red Sea with no repair completed as of the most recent authoritative report (Jul 27 2026); with 'several months' repair timeline from late July, it almost certainly remains unrepaired on Aug 31 2026, satisfying rubric level 2. No market or latency signal was found contradicting the connectivity loss, though rerouting on parallel cables limits but does not eliminate impact.
items.fact: Data Center Dynamics (Jul 27 2026) reported a new break in the PEACE subsea cable in the Red Sea, located ~1,450 km from Zafarnaat Egypt; cause unknown; 'repair is expected to take several months' — indicating the cable remains severed and unrepaired as of that date.

dissent.view: Sept 6 2025 Red Sea multi-cable event (SEA-ME-WE-4, IMEWE, FALCON, EIG) caused measurable latency and Azure disruptions, but those were repaired; rsinc.com Sept 2026 article references a separate Seacom/TGN-Gulf/AAE-1 incident but source reliability is uncertain and may conflate older events.

items.label: AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)
items.rationale: Rubric Level 2 requires 'confirmed curtailment of data-center load, a declared grid emergency, or a power-scarcity-driven moratorium' — all three triggers are simultaneously confirmed: PJM curtailment orders (DOE 202(c)), a Texas statewide connection freeze driven by grid reliability failure at record peak load, and a New York power-scarcity moratorium. IEA (June 2026) corroborates that slow grid connections are forcing developers off-grid to on-site gas, consistent with acute physical constraint.
items.fact: DOE invoked Section 202(c) emergency authority three times in 2026 within PJM, explicitly authorizing curtailment of data center loads with backup generation (confirmed May 18, 2026 order, Utility Dive); Texas governor ordered an effective freeze on new data center grid connections citing grid reliability after ERCOT hit a record 91.1 GW peak on July 22, 2026, with 474 GW of pending interconnection requests (90% data centers) under audit (Morrison Foerster, Aug 2026); New York Executive Order 62 imposes a statewide moratorium on DEC permits for facilities >=50 MW (datacenterbans.com, Aug 2026).

dissent.view: LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition reports a 10% year-over-year decrease in total active queue volume (1,312 GW gen + 749 GW storage as of end-2025), which could suggest marginal easing of queue pressure, though absolute volumes remain historically extreme and the decrease reflects mass withdrawals rather than projects successfully connecting.

items.label: China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
items.rationale: The phosphate export suspension was explicitly extended through August 2026 (announced/confirmed July 29, 2026 - within the trailing 3-month window), constituting a new/prolonged restriction event; the mid-March broadening to NK blends added product categories beyond the original phosphate scope, and urea remains quota-controlled with price floors set by NDRC. This maps to rubric level 2 (NEW or broadened restriction in the trailing 3 months via extension and price-floor mechanism added in May-July 2026). [vintage guard: new read is 2026-07-29 data but the prior applied value was 2026-08-24 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: Fertilizer Daily (July 29, 2026) reports China extended restrictions on phosphate fertilizer exports (DAP, MAP, certain NPK) at least through August 2026; between 50-80% of China export volumes remain restricted per Reuters customs data analysis. Urea quotas (~3 Mt for June-August) were reopened in late May with an NDRC-set floor price of $660/t FOB, but CIQ controls remain active. The phosphate suspension originated from a December 2025 NDRC-directed industry consensus, was broadened in mid-March 2026 to NK blends, and was explicitly extended through August 2026 per Fertilizer Daily July 29 2026.

dissent.view: Urea partially reopened via May 26 quotas (~3 Mt, June-August window) suggesting a partial easing for nitrogen, which could argue for score 1 (restrictions in place but not purely tightened) rather than 2.

items.label: Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: The rubric's level-2 threshold is met by a statewide moratorium enacted: New York's EO 62 is a signed, in-force statewide permitting pause, and Texas's governor-directed grid-connection freeze constitutes a second statewide operational pause — both confirmed physical/regulatory impacts, not mere forecasts. With >10 local jurisdictions also enacting pauses, the WIDESPREAD band is clearly satisfied on multiple criteria.
items.fact: As of end-August 2026, two statewide pauses are in force: (1) New York Executive Order No. 62 (signed July 14, 2026) imposes a moratorium on DEC permitting for data centers ≥50 MW; (2) Texas Gov. Abbott directed PUCT/ERCOT on August 3, 2026 to freeze new grid connections pending a comprehensive audit. Additionally, more than 100 local moratoria have been adopted nationwide, 12 states considered moratorium legislation, and Maine passed a moratorium that was vetoed. Sources: National Law Review (natlawreview.com, July 2026), Houston Public Media (August 3, 2026), DLA Piper (dlapiper.com, July 1, 2026), datacenterbans.com (August 2026).

dissent.view: Maine passed a moratorium bill in April 2026 (which would have been the first statewide enactment) but Governor Mills vetoed it, so it never took effect.
WilmerHale (mid-August 2026) characterises state-level activity as bills introduced in six states with ten bills, potentially undercounting enacted actions vs. introduced bills.

items.label: Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)
items.rationale: A surplus of +96,000t exceeds the +100kt surplus threshold in the rubric, mapping cleanly to band 0 (SURPLUS). The forecast is from ICSG's own April 2026 biannual meeting and is the most current authoritative reading available.
items.fact: ICSG April 2026 'Copper Market Forecast 2026/2027' projects a refined copper market SURPLUS of ~96,000 metric tons in 2026, reversing its October 2025 forecast of a 150,000t deficit; driven by lower-than-expected demand growth (1.6% vs prior 2.1%) and higher secondary/scrap refined output. Source: ICSG April 2026 meeting, Lisbon; corroborated by Recycling Today (28 Apr 2026), ADMIS (24 Apr 2026), IndexBox (Apr/Jul 2026).

dissent.view: ICSG October 2025 forecast projected a 150,000t DEFICIT for 2026 (before scrap supply revision and demand downgrade); J.P. Morgan had projected an even steeper ~330,000t deficit driven by AI/data-center demand.

items.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
items.rationale: D3/D4 coverage across ≈30% of the US Southwest unambiguously meets the rubric's ACUTE threshold (D3-D4 confirmed by the Drought Monitor), and Lake Mead at an all-time record low constitutes a confirmed physical infrastructure impact corroborating the top band. No confirmed fab production curtailment was found, but D3-D4 classification alone is sufficient for value=2 per the rubric.
items.fact: As of August 18, 2026, ~30% of the Intermountain West (AZ, CO, NM, UT, WY) is in Extreme (D3) or Exceptional (D4) drought per the U.S. Drought Monitor; New Mexico alone shows 33% D3 and 3.1% D4 as of Aug 18 2026, and Lake Mead fell to an all-time record-low level on Aug 6 2026 (below 7 million acre-feet vs. 28M+ capacity). Source: drought.gov Intermountain West update Aug 20 2026; droughtmonitor.unl.edu; USDA weather-drought monitor Aug 11 2026.

dissent.view: Arizona specifically shows partial monsoon relief by Aug 25 2026 - D3 essentially negligible (0% meaningful D3 area) in AZ alone, suggesting within-region heterogeneity; AZ may be closer to D2 threshold than D3

items.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
items.rationale: The load-bearing fact is 61 months median IR-to-COD for 2025 COD projects per LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition, published July 2026. The rubric asks for the latest median wait in months — 61 months maps directly and mechanically.
items.fact: LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition (data through end-2025): 'The median U.S. project that reached commercial operation in 2025 spent 61 months in the interconnection queue' — Axis Intelligence citing LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition (axis-intelligence.com, July 2026); corroborated by emp.lbl.gov/queues which states median IR-to-COD was 'over 5 years for projects built in 2025.'

dissent.view: LBNL Queued Up 2025 Edition (data through 2024) reported median duration 'over 4 years' (~48-55 months) for projects built 2018-2024; Loopback Systems cites 55 months for 2024 COD cohort specifically.

items.label: Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)
items.rationale: Fertilizer/sulfur/ammonia AIS outbound flows are confirmed near-zero since the Feb 28 closure and show no material restart through late August; the parent strait tracker rates the strait effectively closed and Brent at ~$88 corroborates the disruption — both conditions required for a score of 2 are met. Partial ambiguity (CENTCOM mine-clearance claim, a brief June post-MoU trickle of ~16 vessels) is insufficient to pull the rating to 1, as the WTO tracker explicitly finds fertilizer flows 'largely at a standstill' with no visible AIS rebound.
items.fact: WTO/ITC Trade Tracker (late-Jun 2026): 'fertilizer-related shipments remain largely at a standstill... AIS-traceable flows remained absent or effectively at zero'; straits.live (Aug 30 2026) rates the strait 'effectively closed' with 3 transits on Aug 23 vs baseline of 85/day; Brent ~$88/bbl (Aug 28). Source: datalab.wto.org/Strait-of-Hormuz-Trade-Tracker (Jun 29 2026) and straits.live (Aug 30 2026).

dissent.view: CENTCOM (CBS News/IranWire, Aug 28 2026) says Hormuz shipping lanes are cleared of IRGC mines and open; Lloyd's List Intelligence (Aug 17-23 window) reported 114 transits week-on-week rise of 30%+ across all cargo — suggesting some movement, which could support a rating of 1.
Bloomberg (Jun 24 2026) reported 16 fertilizer vessels exited post-MoU and volumes 'edging closer to pre-war levels', which if sustained would cap the rating at 1.

items.label: Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
items.rationale: At 26.4% of capacity, Lake Mead is well below the <30% CRITICAL threshold; additionally, at 1,038.87 ft it is approximately 11 ft below Hoover Dam minimum power pool (~1,050 ft), confirming a physical hydropower-generation impact beyond a mere forecast or warning.
items.fact: Lake Mead elevation 1,038.87 ft, storage 6,900,100 AF = 26.4% of the USBR operational capacity of 26,120,000 AF, per Bureau of Reclamation daily gauge data (ReservoirBench citing USBR RISE, Aug 30 2026). This is the reservoir's lowest level since first filling in the 1930s. Elevation is also below Hoover Dam minimum power pool (~1,050 ft).

dissent.view: LakeLevelNow reports ~24% full as of Aug 31 2026, using the NID design capacity of ~28.26 maf rather than the USBR operational 26.12 maf basis; both readings are below 30% so the rating is unaffected.

items.label: Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Three named top-20 mines (Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula, El Teniente/Chilean complex) all have confirmed, currently active production cuts well below nameplate, and multiple major institutions have publicly forecast a material 2026 market deficit — both prongs of the CLUSTER threshold are met. The corroborating LME spread of $150/t and COMEX record of $6.70/lb confirm physical market impact, not merely a forecast.
items.fact: As of August 2026, at least three top-20 copper mines have confirmed, active production cuts: (1) Grasberg (Indonesia, world #2) — Freeport delayed full restart to 2028, targeting only ~65% capacity in H2 2026, with 2026 output ~700 million lb vs pre-incident 1.7 billion lb target (mining.com, May 8 2026); (2) Kamoa-Kakula (DRC, world #3-4) — Ivanhoe cut 2026 guidance to 290,000–330,000 t from original 420,000+ t after 2025 seismic/flood damage, with Q2 2026 industrial action adding 9 days of lost mining (metal.com / natlawreview, July 2026); (3) El Teniente / Chilean mines broadly — Chile Q2 2026 national output down 7.7% YoY, worst multi-mine storm disruption in years affecting El Teniente and Andina, with mine-life extension suspended (techtimes.com / cruxinvestor.com, Aug 2026). Institutions (ING, J.P. Morgan, Benchmark) forecast a 2026 refined copper deficit of 330,000–600,000 kt. LME cash-to-3M spread hit $150/t in August 2026, confirming physical scarcity (discoveryalert.com.au, Aug 2026).

dissent.view: ICSG's refined-market model shows a 2026 surplus, contrasting with ING/JPM/Benchmark deficit calls; ICSG attributes this to secondary/scrap supply offsetting mine losses

items.label: Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)
items.rationale: The Indus Waters Treaty has been unilaterally held 'in abeyance' by India since April 2025 and India is actively rejecting binding arbitration awards — squarely a 'treaty suspended/contested with official threats exchanged' scenario. Pakistan's defence minister issued a conditional war threat but immediately walked it back, and no kinetic action or confirmed deliberate cut-off has occurred, keeping this at Level 1 rather than Level 2.
items.fact: On 2026-08-31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration upheld the Indus Waters Treaty and ordered India to limit dam construction at the Ratle plant; India immediately rejected the ruling, stated the treaty 'will remain in abeyance,' and refused to participate in proceedings — treaty suspended since April 2025 Pahalgam attack (Tribune India, 2026-08-31). Pakistan's defence minister also invoked a war-threat qualifier but explicitly said current developments 'do not warrant military action' (CNBC, 2026-06-22). No deliberate flow cut-off or armed clash confirmed.

dissent.view: Some analysts (CNBC, June 2026) highlight Pakistan's defence minister's 'we will go to war' statement and India's reported short-period flow restrictions via Baglihar/Kishanganga dams as potentially crossing into Level 2 territory; however Pakistan itself clarified no military action is currently warranted and the flow restrictions were not a confirmed sustained cut-off.

items.label: GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)
items.rationale: The rubric's level-2 criterion is 'deadline missed without final rules' — this is precisely the documented status: the July 18, 2026 one-year deadline expired with zero finalized regulations from any of the five required agencies, and new NPRMs are still being filed and accepting comment as of August 2026. No court stay or compliance-failure event is required for this classification; the deadline miss is sufficient and unambiguous.
items.fact: The GENIUS Act Section 13 statutory deadline of July 18, 2026 passed with NO final implementing rules issued by any primary federal regulator (OCC, FDIC, Federal Reserve, NCUA, Treasury/FinCEN/OFAC). As of August 26, 2026, every major rule package remains at the proposed/comment stage; Treasury filed a new NPRM on August 17, 2026 (comments due October 19, 2026), and the OCC targets a final rule by November 2026. Source: The Block, 2026-07-18 ('U.S. regulators reach the GENIUS Act's one-year rulemaking deadline on Saturday without issuing the final regulations'); Federal Register 2026-08-18 doc 2026-16796; crypto.news 2026-08-26.

items.label: SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)
items.rationale: One official extension was formally granted (Feb 25, 2025), satisfying rubric criterion 1 ('SLIPPING'). No second formal extension exists as of Aug 31, 2026, so rubric level 2 ('DELAYED') is not triggered.
items.fact: The SEC granted one formal one-year extension on Feb 25, 2025 (Release No. 34-102487), moving cash clearing from Dec 31, 2025 to Dec 31, 2026 and repo from Jun 30, 2026 to Jun 30, 2027. As of the SEC Commissioner Uyeda August 2026 update (sec.gov, ~Aug 7 2026), no second extension has been announced; the SEC urges industry to prepare 'by the current deadline.' SIFMA exemptive-relief requests (Apr 17, 2026) and reopened comment periods (due Aug 31, 2026) are pending but relate to scope, not a further deadline shift.

items.label: Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)
items.rationale: The cumulative >50bps yield move on fiscal concern meets the rubric's disorderly threshold in magnitude, but auctions continue clearing with bid-to-cover well above 2 and no emergency BOJ operation has occurred, ruling out score 2. Score 1 applies because the funding path is partially unspecified/contested and the 10-year yield is up far more than 25bps on fiscal news while auctions still clear.
items.fact: Japan 10-year JGB yield rose to 2.95% on Aug 31 2026 (TradingEconomics, 2026-08-31), a 30-year high, up ~115bps from pre-Takaichi levels (~1.8% in late 2025) and +12bps over the past month, driven by Takaichi fiscal expansion concerns. Recent auctions cleared with bid-to-cover above 3x (10-year Mar 2026: 3.3; 5-year Aug 18 2026: highest demand since June 2025). No failed auction or emergency BOJ operation confirmed. Funding path remains contested: Takaichi promised no extra net bond issuance (CNBC, May 25 2026) but the MOF is already raising assumed debt-servicing rate to 3.8% for FY2027 (TradingEconomics, Aug 2026).

items.label: Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
items.rationale: The government is actively governing but holds no working majority, has explicitly used Article 49.3, and has survived — not avoided — multiple no-confidence votes; this fits Band 1 (FRAGILE) precisely. No dissolution or PM resignation has occurred since the Second Lecornu government was formed in October 2025.
items.fact: PM Sébastien Lecornu's Second Government (formed Oct 2025) remains in office as of Aug 29, 2026 (Bloomberg, Aug 29 2026). It governs without a parliamentary majority, previously invoked Article 49.3 on the 2026 budget income bill (Jan 20, 2026; France24) and survived multiple no-confidence votes (Oct 16 2025: 271/289 threshold; Jan 23 2026: 269/289; Feb 2 2026: two motions failed), before the 2026 budget passed Feb 2, 2026 (Al Jazeera/Reuters).

items.label: Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)
items.rationale: Two of the three major agencies (Fitch in Sept 2025, S&P in Oct 2025) executed actual one-notch rating cuts on France within the trailing 12-month window, satisfying rubric level 2 (downgrade). Moody's negative outlook alone would already trigger level 1, but the executed cuts by Fitch and S&P mandate the highest band.
items.fact: Fitch downgraded France from AA- to A+ in September 2025; S&P downgraded France from AA- to A+ on October 17, 2025 (spglobal.com/ratings, sourceId/101651950); Moody's kept Aa3 but revised outlook to negative on October 25, 2025 (France24). Fitch reaffirmed A+ with stable outlook on August 28, 2026 (Bloomberg/Euronews). Both Fitch and S&P cuts fall within the trailing 12 months ending 2026-08-31.

items.label: USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
items.rationale: The rubric requires the latest USD share of allocated global FX reserves as a percent; the IMF's own COFER Data Brief for 2026Q1 published July 1, 2026 gives exactly 57.13%, the most recent official data point available as of 2026-08-31. This maps directly and mechanically to the rubric with no ambiguity.
items.fact: IMF COFER Data Brief (data.imf.org, published July 1, 2026): 'The share of US dollar holdings in foreign exchange reserves increased to 57.13 percent in 2026Q1, from 56.42 percent in 2025Q4.'

items.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
items.rationale: The signed figure is +3.5% YoY for July 2026, a moderate positive print reflecting upstream cost-push pressure driven by mining (+16.4% YoY) and raw materials (+6.1% YoY), consistent with input-cost spillover to trading partners. The rubric scores on magnitude; +3.5% is a notable but not extreme positive read, signalling moderate cost-push inflation export risk rather than a deflation shock.
items.fact: In July 2026, China's producer price index for industrial products (PPI) increased by 3.5% year on year — NBS press release t20260810_1965017, released 2026-08-10 (https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202608/t20260810_1965017.html).

items.label: US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
items.rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) are explicitly listed on MOFCOM's export-control entity list as of 22 June 2026, matching rubric level 1 (entity-specific). Multiple corroborating sources confirm the listing is firm-specific, not a categorical sector-wide ban, and market price signals were described as 'muted', capping the read at 1 rather than 2.
items.fact: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 (issued 22 June 2026) added 10 named US entities to China's export control list, including MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth Inc., prohibiting exports of dual-use items to them with immediate effect. The measure is entity-specific, not a sector-wide ban. Sources: Benchmark Minerals (June 25 2026, https://source.benchmarkminerals.com/article/china-targets-us-rare-earth-and-defence-linked-entities-with-dual-use-export-ban); Arnold & Porter advisory (July 2 2026, https://www.arnoldporter.com/en/perspectives/advisories/2026/07/china-imposes-export-control-and-government-procurement-restrictions-on-designated-us-companies); Al Jazeera (June 22 2026, https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/22/china-adds-10-us-firms-including-rare-earth-miner-to-export-control-list).

items.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: MoM gain of 0.6% is well below the 5% spike threshold and the 3-month rise (May–July) is estimated at roughly 2–3%, far below the 10% SPIKING threshold; the index is rising MoM and YoY (multi-year high) but the monthly change is under 3%, squarely mapping to ELEVATED (1). The index is not falling, ruling out 0.
items.fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 131.1 points in July 2026 (released 7 Aug 2026 by FAO), up 0.6% from June 2026 (130.3) and 1.0% above July 2025 — its highest reading since January 2023. Source: https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/fao-food-price-index-edges-up-amid-weather--energy-and-geopolitical-concerns/en

flags.name: Two Hormuz reads disagree on the same strait
flags.message: Gulf fertilizer inputs are rated CUT (2, i.e. closure) but the sea-lane indicator rates the very same Strait of Hormuz only CONTESTED (<=1). They track one physical chokepoint and must agree - align the fertilizer read down to DISRUPTED (1) unless the strait is genuinely closed.

Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)

flags.name: Redemption gates widespread, but HY spreads benign
flags.message: Large-fund redemption gates are rated WIDESPREAD (2) but high-yield spreads are benign. Broad gating usually coincides with visible credit stress; confirm the gates are systemic, not a couple of isolated funds.
